subject: MS
chapter: THE BASIS OF WESLEY'S THEOLOGICAL THINKING
question: Explain the Wesleyan Quadrilateral as the basis of John Wesley's theological thinking.
idealAnswer: The source of John Wesley's theological thinking is four-fold: Scripture, Reason, Tradition and Experience. This is normally referred to as the Wesleyan Quadrilateral, and Wesley appealed to each of these individually in various settings, or often appealed to two or three of them jointly. Scripture came first. Wesley used the Bible as his most basic authority to determine Christian belief and practice; for him Scripture was the sole authority in any doctrinal discourse and should be the constant rule of our tempers, our words and our actions. He called himself Homo Unius Libri, a man of one Book, writing in his Journal that in 1730 he began to study comparatively no book but the Bible, and he allowed no other rule, whether of faith or practice, than the Holy Scriptures. He was convinced of the value of reading Scripture in the original languages and considered it an infallible, totally reliable guide. Reason Wesley used most often in defending doctrinal beliefs. He called it 'this Precious gift of God' and pointed out that Christ and the Apostles never failed to prove every doctrine by Scripture and reason. He held reason to be a legitimate and necessary aid, yet limited in helping us understand all the issues of life and in evaluating all Scripture, and said he was ready to give up every opinion which he could not by calm, clear reason defend. Tradition is the history of the continuing grace by which all Christians live. Wesley affirmed the teachings and examples of the Early Church and the Anglican doctrines, quoting the Anglican Articles of Faith, the Homilies and the Book of Common Prayer. In his sermon 'On Sin in Believers' he insisted that no doctrine can be right unless it is the very same which was from the beginning and based on Scripture; in 'A Short History of Methodism' he said the Methodists' one desire is to be downright Bible Christians, taking the Bible as interpreted by the primitive Church and by the Church of England. Experience Wesley valued as 'plain, practical and experimental religion'. He believed experience is sufficient to confirm a doctrine which is grounded on Scripture; since Scripture did not explicitly settle whether sanctification is instant or gradual, he used experience as his primary criterion. The experience he valued was the wisdom acquired through living, not the spiritual sensations felt at the moment. In conclusion, tradition, experience and reason are closely linked to the study of Scripture but do not displace Scripture as the primary source for faith and practice; the four work together to guide our quest for a vital Christian witness.
keyPoints: Wesley's theological concern was to lead men along the road of salvation.
The four-fold source is Scripture, Reason, Tradition and Experience, called the Wesleyan Quadrilateral.
Scripture is the most basic and sole authority; Wesley was Homo Unius Libri, a man of one Book.
Reason is 'this Precious gift of God', necessary but limited.
Tradition means the Early Church and the Anglican doctrines; no doctrine is right unless it is the same as from the beginning.
Experience confirms a doctrine grounded on Scripture, and settled the question of instant or gradual sanctification.
The experience valued is wisdom acquired through living, not momentary spiritual sensation.
The other three sources never displace Scripture as the primary source for faith and practice.

subject: MS
question: Discuss John Wesley's teaching on humanity as God's gracious creation, with particular reference to the three images of God.
idealAnswer: Wesley's doctrine of man is based on both the Western and Eastern Christian traditions, both of which held that humanity was created in God's image. According to Wesley it was the free grace of God that formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into him a living soul, and the state of man before the Fall was complete perfection. Wesley maintained that God created humanity not as a simple creature but as a complex one, composed of both body and spirit. In his early sermon manuscript 'The Image of God' he observed that man even at his creation was a compound of matter and spirit, and that during this vital union neither part should act at all but together with its companion. The body Wesley described as composed of four elements, namely dust, water, air and fire, duly proportioned and mixed together, and suitably described as 'a little portion of earth', basing his argument on the Genesis account in which God formed man out of the dust of the earth. Yet he insisted the body is not the man: man is an immortal spirit, a spirit made in the image of God, of infinitely more value than the whole material creation. Man is also a soul. Wesley maintained that the body cannot be separated from the soul in the state of existence, yet the death of the body will not involve the death of the soul; the soul will continue to exist when the body dies. He identified the soul or spirit of man with the image of God, and discussed that image under three heads. First, the natural image: man was created in the natural image of God because he had a spirit endued with understanding, with a will and various affections so that he might love, desire and delight in what is good, and with liberty, a power of choosing what was good and refusing what was not. Second, the political image: in creation man was given dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the livestock and all the creatures that move along the ground. Wesley therefore saw man as God's vice-regent upon earth, the prince and governor of this lower world. God does not rule in isolation but rules through His appointed vice-regents; human beings are vice-regents and not regents, because God has not left his creation in our hands to rule absolutely. Third, the moral image: using Ephesians 4:24 as his guide, Wesley stressed that man was made holy as God is holy, merciful as the author of all is merciful, and perfect as his Father in heaven is perfect. As God is love, so man dwelling in love dwells in God and God in him. He was pure as God is pure from every spot of sin, knew not evil in any kind or degree, and was inwardly and outwardly sinless and undefiled. For Wesley the moral image was the principal image.

subject: MS
question: Outline the consequences of the fall and the consequences of original sin according to John Wesley.
idealAnswer: According to Wesley the fall of humanity had a number of unfavourable effects. Adam and Eve experienced both physical and spiritual effects of their sin. Before the Fall humanity had freely received its life from the Creator; now, with the relationship broken, death held sway. Sin brought not only physical death but also pain, sickness and a whole train of uneasy as well as unholy passions and tempers. Adam brought pain, labour and sorrow on himself and all his posterity, together with death, not only temporal but spiritual and eternal. Wesley noted that humanity as God's gracious creation can relate with God, with other humans, with lower animals and with oneself, and that true humanity is where all these relationships are properly expressed. The Fall deprived man of all these relationships. Deprived of his relationship with God, man's faculties became inevitably debilitated and morally depraved: his understanding of God was darkened, his will was seized by wrong tempers and his liberty was lost. While the natural and political images were polluted or lost in part, the moral image was totally lost. Having lost the moral image, Adam sank partly into the image of the Devil, in pride, malice and other evil dispositions, and partly into the image of the brute, having fallen under the power of brutal passions and degrading appetites. The doctrine of original sin arose as the church reflected on the writings of Saint Augustine as to how the fall of Adam and Eve affected the rest of humanity. Original sin is inherited, and Wesley cited Genesis 3:1ff, Psalm 5:5 and Romans 5:12-21 on how it is transferred. From the Romans passage he states that by the disobedience of one man all men were constituted sinners, so that none are exempted from this sinful legacy; all people, infants included, suffer the very same consequences of sin as their progenitors, namely suffering and death. God does not look upon infants as innocent but as involved in the guilt of Adam's sin, otherwise death could not be inflicted upon them. The spiritual legacy Adam bequeathed is that men and women are all gone out of the way of truth and holiness; there is none righteous, no, not one. First, they are born into the world as atheists, having by nature no knowledge of God and therefore no love of God, and so immediately engage in a species of idolatry by worshipping themselves. Second, atheism and idolatry result in pride, the self-glorification whereby men and women think of themselves more highly than they ought. Third, the Adamic inheritance entails self-will: Satan has stamped his own image on our heart in self-will also. Fourth is love of the world, developed under three components: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye and the pride of life. Thus unbelief, pride, self-will and love of the world are the inheritance that Adam and Eve bequeathed to humanity.

subject: MS
question: Explain the doctrine of prevenient grace and state its characteristics according to John Wesley.
idealAnswer: Wesley used the term prevenient grace to mean that grace which goes before any human action for salvation. The beginning of the work of salvation in any human being is God's prevenient grace, which acts before any individual has any thought of turning to the truths of the Christian faith. The import of the doctrine is that the initiative of salvation is with God from the beginning: before the individual ever takes a step, God is there. It may also be called antecedent grace, since God's grace always pre-vents, that is, comes before, and makes possible human response. In Wesley's opinion any person, however apparently ignorant and abandoned, is under the influence of prevenient grace. God comes to humanity first; God seeks us before we ever seek God. The first characteristic is that prevenient grace is available to all. Wesley emphasised 'Free Grace', saying that the grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is free in all and free for all. It does not depend on any power or merit in man, neither in whole nor in part. It is with us from birth, preparing us for new life in Christ, anticipating and preparing men and women for the coming of saving grace, and implying some tendency toward life, some degree of salvation, the beginning of a deliverance from a blind, unfeeling heart. Secondly, it does not wait for the call. We do not have to ask for it, or even desire it; it is simply there. It does not in any way depend on the good works or righteousness of the receiver, not on anything the individual has done or anything he is. Thirdly, God acts first and gives humanity the power to respond, but does not dictate the response. While always holding that the very power by which persons turn to God comes from God as a gift, Wesley also maintained free choice: all are free to choose and, in order to be saved, must play a part by choosing salvation. Prevenient grace inspires and enables but does not force; Wesley understood that we can resist grace. Fourthly, to say that grace is free for all means it is available to everyone, as opposed to the Calvinistic teaching of predestination. The grace of God is not available for a selected few but for all; therefore the outcasts, sinners, the marginalised and the sick could be renewed by the grace of God. It was this emphasis on prevenient grace which was the key factor that held together Wesley's teaching on social ethics, and it places the unbeliever in a position of responsibility for his actions. Fifthly, Wesley sometimes explained the conscience of man in terms of prevenient grace. Finally, prevenient grace gives us a sense of God but is in no sense the totality of God's grace. It only serves to stir us to repentance, which Wesley calls the porch of religion. The entrance to the life of faith is repentance; repentance or conviction of sin always precedes faith, and prevenient grace makes this recognition of the fallen state possible.

subject: MS
chapter: JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
question: What is justification according to John Wesley? Who are justified, and what results follow from justification?
idealAnswer: John Wesley regarded salvation through faith as the fundamental doctrine of the church. He answered the question what justification is by first dealing with what it is not. It is not doing things that are just and righteous, although just and good works are the immediate fruits of justification. It is not God clearing us from the accusations of Satan. Nor is it the clearing of us from the accusation brought against us by the law. Positively, justification is pardon, the forgiveness of sins. It is the act of God the Father whereby, for the sake of the propitiation made by the blood of his Son, he showed forth his righteousness by the remission of the sins that are past. The past sins of the sinner, in thought, word and deed, are covered, and shall not be remembered or mentioned against him any more than if they had not been. God will not inflict on that sinner what he deserved to suffer, because the Son of his love has suffered for him. Justification involves a deliverance from guilt and punishment by the atonement of Christ actually applied to the soul of the sinner now believing on him, and a deliverance from the power of sin through Christ. He who is justified is indeed born again of the Spirit unto a new life, for Wesley did not separate justification from regeneration: in the moment we are justified we are also born of the Spirit. As to who are justified, Wesley pointed out that God justifies the ungodly of every kind and every degree. It is wrong to expect a person to be holy before he is justified. It is not a saint but a sinner that is forgiven; God does not justify the godly but the ungodly, not those who are already holy but the unholy. No sinner is too sinful to be disqualified from God's forgiveness. None of our good works is good enough to justify us before God, so a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law; justifying faith requires a sure trust and confidence that Christ died for our sins. Justification therefore comes by faith alone. Yet to speak of justification by faith alone is not to reject the pursuit of holiness and good works, for the faith which leads to justification must be productive of all good works and all holiness. It is a total commitment of oneself to God. Justification has two dimensions, God's grace and man's responsibility: God justifies by His grace, but for that grace to be effective man must respond of his own free will. Good works cannot save, but they are the inevitable fruit of saving faith. The first result of justification is joy in our faith; whereas prior to 1738 Wesley had the faith of a servant, after that time he had the faith of a son. Another result is the freedom to live as a free person, not perfect but accepted and forgiven by a gracious God. Other results are love, works and generosity, personal and social holiness.

It has two dimensions: God's grace and man's responsibility.
Results: joy in our faith (faith of a son, not of a servant), freedom, love, works, generosity, personal and social holiness.

subject: MS
chapter: JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
question: Distinguish between justification and sanctification in the teaching of John Wesley.
idealAnswer: Wesley himself drew the difference between the two in these words: 'By justification we are saved from the guilt of sin and restored to the favour of God. By sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God.' Justification therefore deals with guilt and with our standing before God; sanctification deals with the power and root of sin and with our restoration to God's likeness. Wesley added that all experience, as well as Scripture, shows this salvation to be both instantaneous and gradual. It begins the moment we are justified by the holy, humble, gentle, patient love of God for man. It gradually increases from that moment as a grain of mustard seed, which at first is the least of all seeds but afterwards puts forth large branches and becomes a great tree, till in another instant the heart is cleansed from all sin and filled with pure love to God and man. Even that love increases more and more till we grow up in all things into Him that is our Head and attain the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. Sanctification is therefore the process of growth into the image of God. God has not only established a relationship with the individual who turns to him, but a process of transformation has begun in that person's life. Sanctification begins the moment a person is justified; it is the inner renewal of a believer by the Holy Spirit, the process where a believer begins to live a holy life. For Wesley the rise of Methodism was the concern for holy living, and the inner work of the Holy Spirit in man is what he described as holy living, which comes by faith in Christ. It is this holy living which Wesley called Christian Perfection. The two must not be separated, for sanctification begins where justification begins; nor must they be confused, as Wesley complained the clergymen of the Church of England did when they spoke of justification either as the same thing as sanctification or as something consequent upon it. Wesley believed justification to be wholly distinct from sanctification and necessarily antecedent to it.

Sanctification saves from the power and root of sin and restores to the image of God.
This salvation is both instantaneous and gradual.
It begins the moment we are justified and increases like a grain of mustard seed.
Sanctification is the process of growth into the image of God, the inner renewal of the believer by the Holy Spirit.
Holy living by faith in Christ is what Wesley called Christian Perfection.
Justification is wholly distinct from sanctification and necessarily antecedent to it.

subject: MS
topic: What Christian Perfection is NOT according to John Wesley
question: State what Christian perfection is NOT and what it is, according to John Wesley.
idealAnswer: Wesley published his understanding of this doctrine in 1766 in his treatise entitled 'A Plain Account of Christian Perfection'. Because the doctrine was so often misunderstood by his critics, the Moravians, the Calvinists and others, and because George Whitefield claimed there is no such perfection on earth, Wesley took great care to state in what sense Christians are not and can never hope to be perfect in this world. Christian perfection does not mean Christians are perfectly perfect. They are not perfect in knowledge; they are not free from ignorance or from mistake, for we are no more to expect any living man to be infallible than to be omniscient. They are not free from infirmities such as weakness or slowness or heaviness of imagination. The perfect Christian is not wholly free from temptation, for the servant is not above his Master. Neither in this sense is there any absolute perfection on earth. Wesley concluded that he never contended for absolute and infallible perfection, nor for sinless perfection, since that is not scriptural, and never spoke of a perfection that perfectly fulfils the whole law and so needs not the merit of Christ. Positively, Wesley made clear he was not speaking of babes in Christ but of adult Christians, though even babes in Christ are so far perfect as not to commit sin. The graces of mature Christians, those strong in the Lord, exceed those of babes in at least two respects. First, they are free from evil thoughts: if the heart is no longer evil, then thoughts involving ill will, lust or envy will no longer be present in the heart. Second, those perfected in love are free from evil tempers. Writing to his brother Charles in 1767 Wesley said, 'By perfection I mean the humble, gentle, patient love of God and man ruling all the tempers, words, and actions, the whole heart by the whole life.' In the same treatise Wesley elaborated that Christian perfection is the giving God all our heart; it is devoting, not a part, but all of our soul, body and substance to God; it is having the mind which was in Christ, and thus enabling us to walk as Christ walked; it is the circumcision of the heart from all filthiness, all inward as well as outward pollution; it is a renewal of the heart in the whole image of God, the full likeness of Him that created it; and it is loving God with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Sanctification is love replacing sin, love conquering every vile passion and temper, and there is nothing higher than this, nothing greater than the love of God reigning in the soul without a rival.

subject: MS
question: Give an account of the life of Charles Wesley from his birth to his conversion in 1738.
idealAnswer: Charles Wesley was born in Epworth on 18th December 1707, the youngest of the three male children to survive to adulthood. He had a less robust constitution than John Wesley, but received the same Epworth training from their mother Susanna Wesley as John did. At the age of five he started formal education and learnt the rules of numbers, scriptures and the catechisms of the Church of England. At about eight he went to Westminster School in 1716, and by virtue of his connection he was elected a student or scholar of Christ Church, Oxford in 1726, continuing his education at Christ Church from Westminster in 1727. He was much influenced in his outlook by his elder brother Samuel Wesley. Originally he did not show any major concern for religion, but by 1729, having been influenced by his elder brother, he became so disappointed with the loose religious life on campus that he proposed to set up a group for reform and asked John Wesley's advice about the system to adopt. In Oxford he gathered round him a devotional group of like-minded students to study Scripture and partake of the Sacrament, called the Holy Club. Writing to Dr. Chandler in 1785 he recalled going to the weekly sacrament and persuading two or three young students to accompany him and to observe the method of study prescribed by the statutes of the University, adding, 'This gained me the harmless nickname of Methodist.' In half a year his brother left his curacy at Epworth and came to their assistance. Once launched on his evangelical career, Charles was as active as John in preaching and in all the other activities of the Holy Club. Charles and John agreed to go out to the new colony of Georgia, John as pastor to the first settlers, while Charles worked as secretary to the Governor of the colony, James Oglethorpe. Charles was persuaded to be ordained so that he could share in John's pastoral duties. Like his brother, the encounter with the Moravians on board the ship and in Georgia greatly influenced his spiritual journey to holiness. Unfortunately Charles felt homesick and found the duties as Oglethorpe's secretary tiresome; his work in the colony was full of abuses and he later found himself out of favour with Oglethorpe. He fell sick, became disillusioned and disheartened, and after less than fourteen months in Georgia he went back to England. Charles was still searching for spiritual holiness when John arrived back in England early in 1738, and in the weeks that followed a new influence came into their lives in the person of Peter Bohler. On 24th February 1738 Bohler visited Charles during one of his periods of intense pain and weakness and prayed at his bedside, asking, 'Do you hope to be saved?' and 'For what reason do you hope it?', to which Charles answered, 'Because I have used my best endeavours to serve God'. Bohler shook his head and said no more. Two months later Charles was still arguing against the idea of instantaneous conversion. Charles Wesley had his spiritual conversion on 21st May 1738 after reading through Luther's commentary on the Book of Galatians, three days before his brother John.

subject: MS
topic: The Use of the Bible in the Methodist Hymns
question: Discuss the use of the Bible in the Methodist hymns of Charles Wesley.
idealAnswer: In the year 1729 John Wesley wrote, 'I began not only to read but to study the Bible', and the result of this devotion is to be seen in every page that he wrote. The two brothers must have had a profound, exact and extensive acquaintance with the Bible; indeed there can hardly be a single paragraph anywhere in the Bible that is not somewhere reflected in the writings of the Wesleys. The hymns in many cases are a mere mosaic of Biblical passages or extracts. A clear example is the stanza beginning 'Behold the servant of the Lord!' (MHB 572:1), where there is a distinct quotation in every line. Its six lines recall six passages in the Authorised Version: 'And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord' (Luke 1:38); 'I will guide thee with Mine eye' (Psalm 32:8); 'If a man love Me he will keep My words' (John 14:23); 'That ye may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God' (Romans 12:2); 'For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from His' (Hebrews 4:10); and 'To fulfill all righteousness' (Matthew 3:15). In 1762 Charles published a collection of Short Hymns on Select Passages of the Holy Scriptures, a kind of devotional commentary in verse, in which we see that the Bible underpins all his hymns. In the four short lines of the first verse of MHB 386, 'O thou who camest from above', there are quotations or echoes of at least five scriptural texts: John 3:31, 1 Kings 18:38, Luke 12:49, 1 Chronicles 21:26 and Leviticus 9:24. This can be done with almost any hymn that he wrote, for all his hymns are steeped in both the language and the ideas of the Bible. Some of his great hymns are based on particular biblical stories. One is how Elijah on Mount Horeb heard God speaking to him in the stillness that followed a great storm (1 Kings 19), which Wesley treats as an allegory of our communion with God, producing a meditation on the work of the Holy Spirit in our hearts (MHB 465). Another, generally thought to be his greatest hymn, is based on Genesis 32:21-32, where Jacob on his journey home wrestles all night with a mysterious figure who turns out to be God. Wesley turns this into an account of the soul agonizing in prayer until it wins through to a confident trust in God's forgiving love, an experience familiar to many of the early Methodist converts, ending 'Thy nature and thy name is Love' (MHB 339). To an age haunted by belief in predestination and the dread of hell-fire the struggle was a real one indeed. Isaac Watts, the other outstanding hymn-writer of the 18th century, declared that this single poem, Wrestling Jacob, was worth all the verses he himself had written. Much of the language of the hymns reveals a mind so steeped in the Bible as to use its language without conscious quotation.

subject: MS
topic: The Sacraments in the Methodist Hymns
question: Describe the place of the great festivals of the Church and of the sacraments in the Methodist hymns.
idealAnswer: Hymns written for use during the major festivals of the Christian year were not common in Wesley's time. John Wesley's most important hymn-book, A Collection of Hymns for Use of the People Called Methodists, published in 1780, contained no section devoted to them. Here too Charles Wesley made a permanent contribution to Christian worship. There are few churches of any denomination which do not celebrate Christmas with 'Hark, the herald angel sing' or Easter with 'Christ the Lord is risen today'. For Ascensiontide there is 'Hail the day that sees him rise' (MHB 221) and for Whit Sunday an expression of renewed confidence in 'Away with our fears' (MHB 278), not to mention a wealth of hymns in the form of prayers to the Holy Spirit. Wesley's firm hold on Christian doctrine is nowhere clearer than in his hymns for Christmas. Among the traditional carols and 19th century hymns sung at that season, his hymns stand out by their lack of sentimentality and their clear understanding of the doctrine of the Incarnation, God become man. Again and again they express the sense of wonder at the paradox of 'our God, contracted to a span, incomprehensibly made man' (MHB 142). 'He laid his glory by, He wrapped him in our clay' was one of his Hymns for Nativity of our Lord, published in 1744, and from the same collection comes 'See the eternal Son of God, a mortal son of man' (MHB 134). As for the sacraments, we need to remind ourselves sometimes that Methodism began as a sacramental as well as an evangelical movement. At a time when the Church of England neglected the Lord's Supper and most parish churches had only three or four celebrations a year, the Wesleys put great emphasis on it as a means of grace. They encouraged their followers to receive the Communion regularly and as frequently as possible, so that the number of Methodists flocking to church for the sacrament sometimes embarrassed the parish clergy. Charles Wesley's Hymns on the Lord's Supper, based on an article by a high church divine, Dr. Daniel Brevint, expressed the Wesleys' high doctrine of the Sacrament as a celebration of Christ's sacrificial love for mankind. For Charles the Lord's Supper was so much more than a mere act of remembrance that he could even speak of Christ's 'real presence' in the Sacrament, praying that Christ would 'show thy real presence here' (MHB 771). It must be noted, however, that the 'real' did not mean 'physical' or imply that the elements of bread and wine were changed in some way; any change that might take place was in the relationship between the worshipper and God. The Wesleys knew from experience that the sacrament was indeed a means of grace, and that for the penitent sinner it might even be the means by which he was converted and found peace with God (MHB 765).
keyPoints: Festival hymns were uncommon in Wesley's time; the 1780 Collection had no section devoted to them.

subject: MS
topic: John Wesley and the Use of Money
question: Outline John Wesley's three rules on the use of money and explain his teaching on each.
idealAnswer: Wesley formulated three simple rules to guide his followers on handling worldly goods. These were: 'Gain all you can, Save all you can and Give all you can'. He cited two reasons for laying down this rule. The first was that most Christians did not know how to deal rightly with money and no one gave them instruction. Secondly, he thought the improper use of a valuable good like money, entrusted to human beings by God, could have far-reaching consequences for both Christians and their neighbours. The first rule, gain all you can, was generally a challenge to earn as much money as possible, however through honest means. The second rule, save all you can, exhorted the Methodist to save money in private treasuries or Bank of England saving accounts and to refrain from all unnecessary spending. Wesley indicated that money was neither good nor evil; in the hands of God's children it becomes nourishment for the hungry, drink for the thirsty and clothing for the naked. All that money could achieve, good or evil, depended on how people used it. The first two rules were only justified through the third rule, give all you can. Wesley drew a boundary between what a person needed to keep and needed to give away: anyone whose income exceeded the necessities of life and personal obligations should give the excess to meet the needs of others. Of those who observed the first two rules and not the third he said they are twofold more the children of hell than ever they were before. Wesley argued that those who impiously, unjustly and cruelly withheld from others what God had entrusted to them for giving aid must be blamed for the needs of others. He saw God as the true owner of all things in heaven and on earth; humans are stewards, and God has provided instructions for the use of what He has given. Those who love money cannot love God or their neighbour. As wealth has increased in the history of the church the mind of Christ has diminished in the same measure; it is only the observance of the third rule, which sets forth the social obligations of possessions, that can convert an increasing income into a blessing. Thus those whose pure intent is to give as much as they can are serving God, their neighbours and their own salvation.

subject: MS
question: Give an account of John Wesley's opposition to slavery.
idealAnswer: The Trans-Atlantic slave trade was started by the Portuguese, and England joined the trade in the latter part of 1550 and became the leading exporter of slaves from Africa to the American market. The profit accruing from the trade was so huge that the king of England, the Cabinet and Parliament did not oppose it, and even the Church of England tolerated it without objection. In 1727 Edmund Gibson, the Bishop of London, rejected the call on slave owners to free slaves who had become Christians, and reprimanded Anglican Christians who freed their converted slaves, appealing to the New Testament (1 Corinthians 7:25 and Colossians 3) as a guarantee for keeping slaves and saying Scripture does not contain any fundamental protest against slavery. In 1774 Wesley published his thoughts upon slavery, in which he criticised the slave trade. He contradicted the widely held view that Blacks were not authentic human beings and contended that the value of a person resides first and foremost in the individual soul, created by God for eternal life, arguing that Blacks as well as Whites possess such a soul. Wesley wrote on the cruelties of capturing, transporting and selling slaves, as well as the inhuman treatment by their owners, which reduced them to a status hardly preferable to beasts of burden. He held the view that both slave owners and those responsible for unjust legislation must expect God's punishment for their misdeeds. He rejected the economic necessity of slavery and maintained that any wealth derived from human bondage was an affront to God, writing: 'Better no trade than trade produced by villainy. It is far better to have no wealth than to gain wealth at the expense of virtue. Better is honest poverty than all the riches brought by the tears, sweat and blood of our fellow creatures.' Wesley supported other anti-slavery leaders such as Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson and William Wilberforce in their campaign against the slave trade. Methodist Conferences in America and England submitted petitions to Parliament calling for the prohibition of slavery, which Wesley saw as a truly Christian plan. In the twilight of his life Wesley and William Wilberforce met for the first time on 24 February 1789, and had important discussions concerning the abolition of slavery; Wesley wrote in his Journal, 'Mr. Wilberforce called upon me, and we had an agreeable and useful conversation.' It is on record that the last letter, written from his deathbed, which epitomised his strong and unabated resolve in the campaign against slavery, was addressed to Wilberforce. Wesley encouraged him to persist against the opponents of abolition and to continue in earnest as the Athanasius contra mundum, Athanasius against the world, writing: 'Unless God has raised you up for this very thing, you will be worn out by the opposition of men and devils. But if God be for you, who can be against you? Go on in the name of God and in the power of His might till even American slavery (the vilest that ever saw the sun) shall vanish away.'

topic: Wesley and the Church of England (Anglican)
question: Discuss the relationship between John Wesley and the Church of England.
idealAnswer: John Wesley was ordained deacon in the Anglican Church by the Bishop of Oxford, John Potter, on 19 September 1725. When he began preaching faith as the basis of salvation, the Anglicans began putting him out of their chapels, for the Anglican belief was that one was saved at the time of baptism, whether infant or otherwise, and that a subsequent experience of faith was simply redundant. Wesley drew a distinction between his sermons and those preached in the Church of England on three points. First, they speak of justification either as the same thing as sanctification or as something consequent upon it, whereas he believed justification to be wholly distinct from sanctification and necessarily antecedent to it. Secondly, they speak of our own holiness or good works as the cause of our justification, whereas he believed neither our own holiness nor good works are any part of our justification, the death and righteousness of Christ being the whole and sole cause. Thirdly, they speak of good works as a condition of justification, necessarily previous to it, whereas he believed no good work can be previous to justification or a condition for it, but that we are justified by faith alone. In spite of these differences Wesley did not separate from the Church of England. At the first Methodist Conference in 1744 the issue of the relationship to the Church of England arose and the Conference decided to maintain unity with it, expressing its willingness to remain obedient to the authorities of the Church unless this obedience would compromise their obedience to God in matters of faith and mission. They declared that they believed and taught the doctrines of the Church of England and that they would obey the bishops and observe the canons whenever this was possible with a safe conscience. In 1752 John Wesley, Charles Wesley and some of the Methodist preachers signed an agreement committing their loyalty to the Church of England. The 1755 Conference revisited the matter under pressure from some quarters to separate and resolved not to separate, as it was in no way expedient, and the 1756 Conference closed with a solemn declaration of their purpose never to separate. In 1758 Wesley declared his reasons: whether it was lawful or not, it was by no means expedient to separate from the established church. He believed that normally God seeks to revive his church from within and that schism is only necessary in the desperate situation where the true witnesses are thrust out; schism was tragic, for the mission of the church was closely associated with her spirit of unity, and division destroys that spirit. Charles Wesley was strongly against separation and at the 1763 Conference warned that all preachers and people should go to church, receive the sacraments at every opportunity, and refrain from calling their society a church or their preachers ministers. In August 1780 Wesley asked Bishop Lowth of London to ordain some of the Methodist preachers to minister in America, but he refused. Therefore in September 1784 Wesley ordained Dr. Thomas Coke as superintendent and Richard Whatcoat and Thomas Vasey as Elders for America, and in 1785 he ordained John Pawson, Thomas Hanby and Joseph Taylor to minister in Scotland. He told the 1786 Conference that those ordinations were not separations from the Church of England or the Church of Scotland, and from 1785 to 1788 he ordained more preachers for Antigua, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the West Indies, and in 1788 Alexander Mather as superintendent for England, followed in 1789 by Henry Moore and Thomas Rankin. Still Wesley did not regard these ordinations as separation and urged the Methodists to attend the Church of England for communion. However, Methodism was not accepted in England as a society within the Church of England.
keyPoints: Wesley was ordained deacon by John Potter, Bishop of Oxford, on 19 September 1725.
The Anglicans put him out of their chapels because they held one was saved at baptism.
Three differences: justification distinct from and antecedent to sanctification; good works no part of justification; no good work previous to or a condition of justification.
The first Methodist Conference (1744) decided to maintain unity with the Church of England.
In 1752 the Wesleys and some preachers signed an agreement of loyalty; the 1755 and 1756 Conferences refused to separate.
In 1758 Wesley gave his reasons: separation was by no means expedient; schism is tragic and destroys the spirit of unity.
Charles Wesley warned the 1763 Conference against calling the society a church or the preachers ministers.
After Bishop Lowth refused in 1780, Wesley himself ordained Coke, Whatcoat and Vasey in 1784, and others later, yet denied that this was separation.

question: Trace the process by which the Methodist Church Ghana adopted Episcopal Leadership, and describe the Proclamation Service.
idealAnswer: Episcopal Leadership of the church is the system whereby the church is led by bishops. In 1990 the Kumasi District Synod started the discussions that would move the Methodist Church Ghana towards Episcopal Leadership. That same year the Chairman of the District, Rt. Rev'd Samuel Asante Antwi, submitted a proposal to the Methodist Conference meeting at Koforidua. The Kumasi Synod requested Conference to adopt district autonomy with Episcopal Leadership involving a threefold ministry of bishops, elders and deacons. The 1991 Conference directed District Synods to discuss the Episcopal system and submit their reports to the 1992 Conference. The 1992 Conference discussed the system but rejected the idea because there were not enough reports on it from the districts: Winneba, Sekondi and Northern Ghana districts did not submit any report; Cape Coast and Akim Oda were not in favour; Koforidua and Tarkwa were in favour but pointed out that the Church's structures be maintained; Accra was in favour but asked for adequate preparation; and it was only Kumasi and Sunyani who were fully in favour of the system. In 1992 the Kumasi District implemented the idea of a separated Chairman as a move towards the Episcopal system, and Kumasi was followed by the Sunyani District. The 1995 Conference revisited the proposal and directed the 1996 Synods to do more discussions on it, and the 1996 Conference at Winneba directed districts to give more education on the system to members of the Church. The process was intensified when Rt. Rev Samuel Asante Antwi became President of the Methodist Church Conference in 1997. The thirty-eighth Methodist Church Ghana Annual Conference, held at the Wesley Methodist Church, Koforidua, from 18 to 25 August 1999, adopted the Episcopal Leadership for the Methodist Church Ghana. The Episcopal leadership system as it operates in Ghana Methodism is a Biblical Pattern of Episcopacy, unlike the Roman Catholic type which is Monarchical. Following the adoption, Conference mandated the General Purposes Council to make the transitional arrangements. A Service of Proclamation was held on Sunday, 23 January 2000 at the Wesley Methodist Church, Asafoatse Nettey Road, Accra, at 8.30am. The main officiating clergy were the Most Rev. Dr. Samuel Asante Antwi, the Presiding Bishop of the Methodist Church Ghana, and His Eminence Sunday Mbang, the Prelate of the Methodist Church Nigeria and Vice Chairman of the Executive Committee of the World Methodist Council. In attendance were some of the Bishops of the Catholic and Anglican Churches in Ghana and other Heads of Churches. Changes in offices were proclaimed. The President of the Conference became the Presiding Bishop, referred to as 'The Most Reverend...'; the Vice President became the Lay President; the Secretary of Conference became the Administrative Bishop, referred to as 'The Right Reverend...', responsible for the administrative affairs of the Church; the Districts became Dioceses; the Chairmen and General Superintendents of Districts became Diocesan Bishops, referred to as 'The Right Reverend...'; a Superintendent Minister is referred to as 'The Very Reverend...'; all ordained ministers are Elders, referred to as 'The Reverend...'; and all probationers or ministers-on-trial are Deacons, also referred to as 'The Reverend...'.
keyPoints: Episcopal Leadership is the system whereby the church is led by bishops.
